title: Private Equity: Explained
author: Dev Singh
body:
INTRODUCTION TO PRIVATE EQUITY

Private equity (PE) refers to investment firms that specialise in the acquisition and restructuring of privately held companies that are not listed on public stock markets. These investment funds are managed by private equity firms, whose major goal is to raise the profitability of the companies they buy through restructuring and operational improvements. In 2023, PE firms managed an astounding $8.2 trillion in assets globally, demonstrating its significant impact on the global financial markets as well as the broader economy. Despite the industry's growth, impact, and influence, many are still unaware of how private equity operates and its contribution to shaping 21st-century economics.

Private equity is distinguished by its active management style, since PE firms frequently collaborate closely with the companies they purchase to execute changes targeted at increasing value. When a business becomes more lucrative or efficient, the private equity firm often sells it at a profit, either directly or through an initial public offering (IPO), where a private company offers its shares to the public for the first time. This allows the private equity firm to sell its stake at a higher price, benefiting from the changes they implemented to increase the company's value.

PRESENCE IN THE MARKET

Private equity firms invest in different sectors and regions; however, there are discernible investment patterns that can be analysed.

The data shows the percentage of PE firm investment deals by sector in both the USA and Europe. In the US, the service sector is responsible for the most investment deals by PE, reaching figures higher than pre-COVID. This has also meant an overall decline in investment in consumer goods, falling to under 10% â€” a shift explained by the change in consumer behaviour post-pandemic towards digitalisation. Online services became more prominent in daily life, and the overwhelming demand incentivised PE firms to invest. Both regions have also seen an increase in technology investment deals since 2016. This is likely because tech companies tend to achieve higher growth than other industries: over the last year, the technology sector grew by over 30%, beating the overall market growth of approximately 20%, thus luring in private equity investors with a clear profit incentive.

EFFECTS ON THE ECONOMY

The economic impact of PE firms increasing their investment in technology can be represented using Solow's Growth Model. The investment of private equity firms in technology causes both the quality and quantity of capital in the economy to increase, making capital more efficient and productive and raising output significantly. The increase in output driven by greater efficiency may lead to broader economic growth. However, the substitution of capital for labour could also lead to technological unemployment, potentially harming the standard of living for displaced workers.

INVESTMENT STRATEGIES

Private equity firms have several different strategies for investing. One of the most popular is the leveraged buyout (LBO). In an LBO, debt funds the acquisition of the target firm, and the arrangement of this debt influences the possible risks and rewards for both lenders and acquirers. The utilisation of debt makes the investment risky, as financial leverage amplifies both gains and losses.

Like all forms of investment, LBOs can generate economies of scale, lowering the average cost per unit and providing consumers with higher-quality yet more affordable goods and services. Additionally, economies of scale may lead to an increase in wages and employment as the firm's profits grow alongside its size and market share â€” raising disposable income and consequently aggregate demand.

However, high liabilities can significantly amplify losses. In 2005, KKR Group et al. acquired Toys R Us for $6.6 billion, using $5 billion in debt. Under KKR's ownership, Toys R Us failed to grow significantly enough to service its debt. This led to the company filing for bankruptcy and closing all of its remaining 700 US outlets, laying off over 30,000 employees in 2018. Though the brand eventually reopened, the poorly managed acquisition highlights the obvious risks of private equity.

FINAL EVALUATION

Many question the morality of burdening a firm with extreme levels of debt, risking the employment and livelihoods of thousands of workers. A publicly owned company would not have such extreme debt-to-equity ratios, which further questions the regulation and power of private equity firms. That said, private equity firms generate vast economic output, accounting for 12 million jobs and approximately 6.5% of United States GDP â€” justifying their place in the financial sector and their value to the economy.

HAVE A THINK

  • How could you demonstrate the investment by private equity firms into technology using a Production Possibility Frontier?

  • How will private equity firms be affected by the US Federal Reserve slashing interest rates?

  • In what ways does the use of leverage in LBOs contribute to achieving economies of scale, and how can this relationship be illustrated in an economic diagram?

title: LVMH's Struggle
author: Ioan Dueymes
body:
LUXURY'S NEW REALITY

LVMH â€“ MoÃ«t Hennessy Louis Vuitton â€“ the world's most successful luxury conglomerate and the highest-valued French company, has recently been subject to sharp share-price adjustments. Its share price lost no less than 36% of its value in the first quarter of 2025 alone, erasing almost â‚¬100 billion of market capitalisation. This dramatic decline is not only the result of economic vulnerabilities but also caused by an escalating trade war with the United States, one of the group's most crucial export markets.

THE PRICE OF PROTECTIONISM

American tariffs on European imports â€” a protectionist policy specifically targeting high-value items such as leather handbags, beauty products, and fine wines â€” have heavily affected LVMH's key sales. With these new barriers to trade, the price of LVMH goods in the US has risen dramatically, resulting in a sharp reduction in the quantity demanded.

This is a textbook example of a cost-push shock: tariffs increase production and selling costs, shifting the supply curve to the left, raising the equilibrium price and lowering output. Although price elasticity of demand (PED) tends to be relatively inelastic for luxury items â€” where consumers are less responsive to price changes â€” even a minor decline in quantity sold at such high price points has a greater than expected impact on total revenue.

INCREASING SUPPLY COSTS

The firm's average costs have increased not only because of tariffs but also because of persistent supply-side pressures. French labour costs and broader EU-wide inflationary trends have risen, and exchange rate volatility has inflated the price of imported resources. The euro's weakness against the dollar has made imported raw materials more costly, while any currency benefit to European exports is counterbalanced by the rise in US import tariffs.

ARNAULT'S PROPOSAL

In response, CEO Bernard Arnault has criticised the European Commission's inability to address growing trade tensions and signalled a potential change in strategy. Arnault has suggested ramping up foreign direct investment (FDI) into the United States to overcome tariffs and manufacture goods locally. Although this could restore price competitiveness in the US market, it risks eroding the company's premium "Made in France" image â€” one of the firm's key drivers of demand. High-income consumers value the origin, tradition, and craftsmanship of the product deeply, and shifting production could therefore dissolve these brand associations.

RIPPLE EFFECTS ON THE FRENCH ECONOMY

The repercussions for the French economy are substantial. In France, LVMH is not only a luxury brand but also a key export earner. A weakening in demand for these exports could further increase the country's current account deficit. It also impacts national income through the circular flow of income, with lower export revenue leading to reduced investment inflows and lower employment in high-skilled manufacturing sectors. This is a clear example of derived demand: demand for skilled labourers and specialist materials is derived from the final demand for luxury items. A fall in luxury demand therefore produces a negative multiplier effect, impacting the French economy far beyond the luxury sector alone.

POLICY OPTIONS: TARIFFS VS. SUBSIDIES

To offset these pressures, different policies are being debated. The EU may impose retaliatory tariffs to protect domestic industries, or extend targeted subsidies to companies hurt by external trade shocks. These solutions, however, involve trade-offs. Retaliation can worsen the conflict and lower overall welfare, while subsidies involve an opportunity cost â€” removing public money from healthcare, education, or infrastructure. Policymakers therefore face the familiar dilemma between free trade and protectionism: trading the long-run benefits of liberalisation against the short-run need to shield domestic industries from instability.

INVESTORS' REACTION

Investor confidence in LVMH has also been shaken. The falling share price has had repercussions across the CAC 40 index, driving broader market volatility. This demonstrates the outsized influence LVMH carries on financial markets: its performance affects investor confidence more widely, making investors more cautious about other European companies that rely heavily on international sales and are vulnerable to unpredictable policy shocks beyond their control.

GLOBAL TRADE UNCERTAINTY: THE WTO

The enforcement of fair trading conditions is further complicated by the World Trade Organization (WTO), which promotes trade liberalisation but whose enforcement can be slow and, in some cases, influenced by geopolitics. This means that powerful countries like the US can still impose unfair tariffs without immediate repercussions. The resulting environment of uncertainty reduces long-term investment and disrupts the supply of goods and services, making it harder for luxury brands like LVMH to maintain the consistency and trust that underpin their premium positioning.

CONCLUSION

LVMH's recent difficulties in the luxury goods market demonstrate the profound consequences that macroeconomic policy, supply-side pressures, and geopolitical factors can have on even the largest firms. Tariffs, currency swings, and complex global trade rules are forcing companies to rethink their strategies. Businesses like LVMH must now balance immediate pressures against the imperative of protecting a long-term brand identity built over generations.

HAVE A THINK

  • How far should a luxury firm go in adapting its supply chain before it risks damaging the brand identity that drives its demand?

  • What does LVMH's situation reveal about the limits of free trade institutions like the WTO in an era of rising nationalism?

  • Could the negative multiplier effect from LVMH's decline accelerate France's existing fiscal crisis, and how should policymakers respond?

title: The Volatility of Gold
author: Ara Malkasinian
body:
GOLD'S RISE AMID ECONOMIC UNCERTAINTY

Gold has long been regarded as a safe-haven asset, particularly in times of economic distress. Yet its price has been incredibly volatile in recent times. In April 2025, the international gold market hit record highs, with gold trading at $3,357 per ounce â€” a rise of over 35% in the last year alone, backed by a rare confluence of geopolitical tensions, shifting monetary policies, and surging demand for safe-haven assets.

WHY IS THE PRICE OF GOLD SO VOLATILE?

A fundamental explanation of such volatility rests in gold's dual status: it is both a financial instrument and a physical commodity. Economically, the supply of gold is inelastic. Gold mining is a slow, capital-intensive process, and short-run increases in demand are difficult to match with corresponding increases in output. Demand, by contrast, is extremely responsive to shifts in market sentiment.

When inflation expectations rise or global financial markets become volatile, safe-haven assets â€” most notably gold â€” experience sudden surges in demand, triggering abrupt price spikes. With an inelastic supply curve held constant, a rightward shift in the demand curve produces a sharp rise in the equilibrium price, illustrating precisely why gold moves so dramatically in response to global events.

THE US EFFECT: HOW AMERICA'S POLICY IS DRIVING VOLATILITY

The surge in early 2025 was primarily driven by increased geopolitical tensions, aggressive US tariff measures against Chinese imports, and growing fears of a global economic slowdown. Goldman Sachs attributes these factors to gold acting as the preferred hedge against policy error, upgrading its 2025 projection to $3,700 per ounce â€” with a bullish case of $4,500 per ounce in the event of a global recession. J.P. Morgan, meanwhile, attributed the sustained rally to ongoing central bank accumulation.

As global trade declined and business and consumer confidence weakened due to US tariffs, aggregate demand shifted left, reducing real GDP. With tariffs also generating inflationary pressure, investors began demanding more gold as a hedge â€” pushing its price further upward and reinforcing the flight to safety.

CENTRAL BANKS AND STRATEGIC RESERVES

Another major driver of gold price fluctuations is the behaviour of central banks, particularly in emerging markets. The People's Bank of China has actively added to its gold holdings to diversify away from the US dollar, accumulating more than 200 tonnes over the past year alone. As the World Gold Council reports, this surge in institutional demand has created a physical shortage in the international gold market, constricting supply and placing sustained upward pressure on prices. It also reinforces gold's status as a financial instrument beyond its industrial or retail applications.

DIGITAL DISRUPTION AND THE RISE OF ALTERNATIVES

A more recent factor influencing gold's volatility is the growing popularity of digital assets like cryptocurrencies. Many younger investors now view Bitcoin as "digital gold" â€” a store of value during periods of uncertainty. When crypto markets perform well, some investors shift away from traditional gold, reducing demand. When confidence in digital assets collapses, money flows back into gold, causing sudden price spikes. This back-and-forth adds a new layer of instability to an already volatile market, particularly as technology plays an increasingly significant role in investment decisions.

SPECULATION FOR THE FUTURE

Looking forward, gold prices are likely to remain elevated as geopolitical instability, rising national debt levels, and investor uncertainty push more people towards safe-haven assets. With central banks continuing to diversify away from the US dollar and new retail investors entering the market through online platforms, demand is likely to stay high while supply remains constrained. This imbalance could sustain upward pressure on prices throughout the next decade.

CONCLUSION

Gold's price is volatile as a result of a complex combination of inelastic supply, rapidly shifting demand, global speculation, and macroeconomic uncertainty. In the future, gold is likely to remain responsive to real interest rates, geopolitical tension, and central bank action â€” acting as both a safeguard and a hazard in an unpredictable global economy.

HAVE A THINK

  • Is gold still a reliable safe-haven asset in a world where digital alternatives are gaining credibility?

  • How does the inelasticity of gold supply limit governments' and firms' ability to respond to sudden surges in demand?

  • Could central banks' shift away from the US dollar and towards gold mark the beginning of a longer-term transformation in the global monetary system?

title: Derivatives 101
author: Finlay Davison
excerpt: The Fine Print Behind Market Moves
body:
MANAGING UNCERTAINTY IN A WORLD OF CHANGING PRICES

In economics, prices are constantly changing â€” whether it's the cost of wheat, the value of stocks, or the exchange rate between currencies. Businesses, investors, and policymakers are always looking for ways to manage these changes and reduce uncertainty. This is where derivatives come in.

A derivative is a financial contract that derives its value from another "underlying" asset, such as a commodity, stock, or interest rate. In simpler terms, a derivative is a bet on the future price of something. While derivatives play a massive role in modern finance and economics â€” helping businesses manage risks and traders generate returns â€” they also bring complexity and risk that must be carefully understood.

WHY DERIVATIVES EXIST: TWO CORE CONCEPTS

At their core, derivatives exist because of two fundamental economic principles.

Risk management: Businesses and investors use derivatives to protect themselves from unexpected price changes, which is especially important as supply and demand are always shifting.

Price discovery: Derivatives markets help determine fair prices for assets by incorporating information about future expectations, making markets more efficient overall.

THE FOUR MAIN TYPES OF DERIVATIVES

Futures: A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a fixed price on a specific future date. These contracts are widely used in commodity markets â€” oil, wheat, gold â€” as well as financial markets. Futures help stabilise markets by reducing uncertainty. Farmers use wheat futures to secure a price before harvest, protecting themselves from sudden price drops. Airlines use oil futures to manage fuel costs, keeping ticket prices stable for consumers.

Options: An option gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined price within a specific timeframe. Options allow businesses and investors to limit potential losses. A well-known early example comes from Thales of Miletus, who used his knowledge of astronomy to predict a bumper olive harvest. Before the season, he paid a small fee to secure the right to use local olive presses. When demand for the presses soared, he rented them out at a much higher price, making a significant profit.

Swaps: A swap is an agreement between two parties to exchange financial instruments, often involving interest rates or currencies. These are essential in international finance. A European company trading in the US might use a currency swap to hedge against exchange rate volatility, ensuring stable profits and predictable costs.

Forwards: A forward contract is like a futures contract but privately negotiated rather than exchange-traded. These are commonly used by businesses seeking tailored risk management. Premier League football clubs, for example, often use forward contracts to lock in exchange rates when signing international players, protecting against currency movements inflating transfer costs.

THE RISKS OF DERIVATIVES: THE 2008 CRISIS CASE STUDY

Some derivatives allow investors to control large sums of assets with only a small upfront payment. While this can boost profits, it also dramatically increases risk â€” as the 2008 financial crisis made devastatingly clear.

At the centre were credit default swaps (CDSs) â€” derivatives that acted like insurance on loans. If a borrower failed to repay, the CDS seller had to compensate the buyer. Banks used CDSs to protect themselves, but many also used them to speculate on whether loans would fail.

These swaps were often tied to mortgage-backed securities (MBSs) â€” bundles of home loans, many of which were high-risk "subprime" loans given to borrowers with poor credit histories. When thousands of borrowers defaulted, the value of MBSs collapsed. Financial giants like Lehman Brothers and AIG, who had sold huge quantities of CDSs without sufficient reserves, were devastated.

Lehman went bankrupt. AIG required a $180 billion US government bailout. The damage spread rapidly across Europe and Asia. Credit froze, confidence collapsed, and a global recession followed. This case study shows how derivatives, when poorly understood or inadequately regulated, can turn from powerful financial tools into global economic threats.

CONCLUSION

Derivatives are far more than just financial contracts â€” they are fundamental to how modern economies function. By managing risk, stabilising prices, and facilitating trade, they reduce uncertainty and increase market efficiency. However, if misused, they can contribute to financial crises of extraordinary scale. Understanding derivatives provides insight into how businesses make decisions, how markets function, and how global trade is shaped by financial instruments â€” making them an essential subject for any student of economics.

HAVE A THINK

  • Should derivatives markets face tighter regulation after the 2008 crisis, or would that risk reducing the economic benefits they provide?

  • How did the use of leverage in credit default swaps transform a localised housing market problem into a global financial crisis?

  • Can price discovery in derivatives markets ever be truly efficient, or does speculation always introduce distortions?

title: Businessman of the Month: Jack Ma
author: Yash Nigam
body:
WHO IS JACK MA?

Jack Ma is a Chinese entrepreneur, philanthropist, former English teacher, and the visionary founder of Alibaba Group â€” one of the world's largest e-commerce, retail, internet, and technology conglomerates. Under Ma's leadership, Alibaba transformed China's digital economy and opened global markets to millions of small businesses.

Known for his charisma, optimism, and bold thinking, Jack Ma became the face of China's internet boom and was regularly ranked among the world's most influential people by TIME, Forbes, and Fortune. Despite stepping down from Alibaba in 2019, his legacy continues to shape global business, entrepreneurship, and digital innovation.

EARLY LIFE

Jack Ma, born Ma Yun in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province in 1964, came from humble beginnings. His family had limited financial means, and his early academic performance was average. However, Ma developed an unusual passion for the English language through frequent interactions with Western tourists at a hotel near his home. Every morning before school, he would ride his bike for miles to offer free guided tours to English-speaking visitors â€” an experience that not only improved his language skills but broadened his worldview considerably.

Despite failing the Chinese university entrance exams twice, he persisted and was finally accepted into Hangzhou Normal University, earning a degree in English in 1988. After graduation, he worked as an English teacher, earning around $12 a month.

In 1995, during a trip to the United States as a translator, Ma was introduced to the internet for the first time. Shocked to find no Chinese websites in search results, he sensed a massive opportunity. That trip sparked the idea that would eventually become Alibaba.

ALIBABA: THE SUCCESS STORY

In 1999, Jack Ma co-founded Alibaba Group in his apartment with 17 friends and an initial investment of $60,000. The goal was to create an online marketplace where small Chinese manufacturers and suppliers could connect directly with buyers around the world. At the time, few people in China had internet access, and fewer believed in e-commerce â€” but Ma's unwavering belief in technology's potential kept the team motivated through the difficult early years.

The early days were tough. Ma faced rejection from multiple investors, including Silicon Valley venture capitalists who didn't understand the Chinese market. SoftBank's $20 million investment in 2000 gave Alibaba the runway it needed. The group later launched Taobao in 2003 to compete with eBay in China, and introduced Alipay â€” a digital payment platform that would become the backbone of China's cashless economy.

In 2014, Alibaba went public on the New York Stock Exchange, raising $25 billion â€” the largest IPO in history at the time. As of 2024, Alibaba serves over one billion active users, and Jack Ma's personal wealth peaked at over $60 billion, making him one of Asia's wealthiest individuals.

PHILANTHROPY

After retiring from Alibaba in September 2019, Ma shifted his focus to education and philanthropy. Through the Jack Ma Foundation, he has committed hundreds of millions of dollars to rural education, environmental protection, public health, and entrepreneurship.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, he donated millions of face masks, test kits, and ventilators to over 150 countries. He has also championed women in business, youth entrepreneurship, and international education initiatives â€” work he describes as more meaningful than building a technology empire.

WHAT'S NEXT?

Though Jack Ma has maintained a lower public profile since 2020 â€” particularly following regulatory scrutiny in China â€” his influence remains deeply embedded in the global technology ecosystem. As Alibaba navigates a changing Chinese tech landscape, Ma's legacy continues to inspire entrepreneurs worldwide. His ambition now is not just about building technology empires, but about building minds and ensuring that technology serves humanity for the greater good.

HAVE A THINK

  • What does Jack Ma's journey from English teacher to tech billionaire reveal about the role of entrepreneurship in driving economic development?

  • How did Alibaba's rise change the competitive dynamics of global e-commerce, and what are the implications for smaller markets?

  • Should governments impose stricter regulation on technology giants like Alibaba, or does doing so risk stifling the innovation that drives growth?

title: Spotify vs Apple: The Oligopoly in the Music Industry
author: Shivam Bakhda
excerpt: The Oligopoly in the Music Industry
body:
INTRODUCTION

In the 21st century, the music business has moved from the physical sale of albums and singles to a world where streaming now contributes 84% of the revenue generated by the music industry. The market is dominated by two key players: Spotify and Apple Music. These two companies have created an oligopoly â€” a market structure where a handful of firms dominate large parts of the market. This article explores the market conditions, the economics of the streaming oligopoly, and the impact of these dynamics on consumers, artists, and the wider industry.

THE CURRENT MARKET AND MARKET SHARE

The music streaming industry is massive, with global revenue currently at $17.5 billion, more than one trillion songs streamed on demand in the US alone, and over 600 million subscribers worldwide. As of 2024, Spotify holds over 30% of the global market share, followed by Apple Music with approximately 15%. Amazon Music accounts for 13%, YouTube Music for 9%, and other smaller services share the remainder. These are the characteristics of a true oligopoly â€” dominant firms wielding significant power over pricing, regulation, and the broader direction of the industry.

SPOTIFY'S FREEMIUM MODEL

Spotify began as a Swedish start-up in 2006 under CEO Daniel Ek. Its key competitive advantage lies in the freemium model: free listening with advertisements and limited features, with a premium upgrade available at approximately $10 per month. This creates a low barrier to entry for new users, making it particularly effective in price-sensitive markets.

Spotify now has approximately 422 million global users, of which 188 million have converted into paid subscribers. The platform has invested heavily in personalised experiences, with recommendation algorithms powering features such as Discover Weekly, Daily Mix, and Smart Shuffle â€” all designed to deepen engagement and reduce churn.

APPLE'S ECOSYSTEM INTEGRATION MODEL

Apple Music's competitive advantage lies in the leverage of Apple's broader ecosystem. Since its launch in 2015, it has been seamlessly integrated with the iPhone, iPad, and MacBook, allowing it to gain millions of users immediately through pre-installation. Once a user is embedded in the Apple ecosystem, switching costs are high â€” making Apple Music particularly sticky.

Unlike Spotify, Apple Music does not offer a freemium tier. It is a fully premium service, differentiating itself through higher-quality audio, exclusive releases, and curated content rather than price accessibility.

THE IMPACT ON COMPETITION

The dominance of Spotify and Apple Music creates serious barriers to entry for new competitors. Their vast user bases, comprehensive catalogues, and long-term licensing agreements with major record labels make it extremely costly for new entrants to challenge them. Network effects compound this advantage: the more users a platform has, the more valuable its personalisation algorithms become â€” creating a self-reinforcing cycle that is very difficult to break into.

THE IMPACT ON CONSUMERS AND ARTISTS

For consumers, the oligopoly has driven meaningful innovation. Both platforms compete through new features, and standard subscriptions remain relatively affordable. However, the market also constrains consumer choice: exclusive content deals mean certain performances or releases are only available on one platform, forcing listeners to choose or pay for both.

For artists, the picture is more troubling. Both platforms use a pro-rata model in which royalties are distributed as a share of total streams â€” a system that disproportionately benefits major artists with millions of streams while leaving independent musicians with very little. In 2023, the average payout per stream on Spotify fell between $0.003 and $0.005. Apple Music pays approximately $0.01 per stream â€” slightly higher, but still requiring millions of streams to generate substantial income. The British Government's DCMS Committee has raised serious concerns, noting that while UK music streaming generates over $1 billion in revenue, artists can receive as little as 13% of the income generated.

CONCLUSION

Spotify and Apple Music's competition has created a powerful oligopoly in the music streaming market. While this promotes innovation and benefits consumers in some respects, it simultaneously restricts new entrants and holds significant negative implications for smaller artists. As these platforms continue to grow, oligopolistic control is likely to deepen â€” raising important questions about the future of competition, fair compensation, and creative diversity in the music industry.

HAVE A THINK

  • Is the pro-rata streaming model fundamentally unfair to independent artists, or is it a reasonable reflection of market demand?

  • Could a new entrant ever meaningfully challenge Spotify and Apple Music, or are the barriers to entry now too high?

  • Should governments intervene in the music streaming industry, and if so, what form should that intervention take?

title: The Stall of Electric Vehicles
author: Jincheng Zhou
body:
THE RISE OF ELECTRIC VEHICLES

Electric vehicles (EVs) are one of the fastest-growing markets of the 21st century. Valued at $380 billion USD in 2022, the global EV market is expected to grow to $1.89 trillion USD by 2032. While EVs were invented in the 1890s, recent technological advancements and growing environmental concerns have caused public interest to surge. Unlike internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, EVs are marketed as environmentally friendly and offer significantly lower operating costs â€” consumers spend roughly 60% less annually on fuel.

Between 2019 and 2022, the market share of EVs in global new car sales increased by 438%, with global consumer spending reaching approximately $400 billion USD in 2022. In response, firms have planned to invest $616 billion USD in the EV industry between 2023 and 2027.

THE SLOWDOWN IN EV DEMAND GROWTH

Despite these projections, demand growth has been slowing over the past two years. Sales have been growing at a slower pace since Q2 2023, and even decreased in Q1 2024.

It is important to note the distinction: demand growth has been slowing, not demand itself. Consumers are still buying more EVs each quarter â€” just at a lower rate of increase compared to the year before.

WHY IS DEMAND GROWTH SLOWING?

Early EV buyers were often wealthier, environmentally conscious consumers willing to pay a premium and position themselves as pioneers. As EVs moved towards the mass market, the next wave of consumers proved far more price-sensitive and practical-minded, slowing demand growth significantly.

EVs are also more expensive to insure due to the high cost of their components â€” notably the battery, which accounts for over 30% of the vehicle's total cost. Its production requires a mix of rare raw materials, further inflating the price through a costly extraction process.

Recently, Volvo abandoned its target of exclusively selling EVs by 2030 due to the global slowdown in demand. Meanwhile, Apple cancelled its "Titan" EV project after spending over ten years and $10 billion USD in development â€” a stark signal of the difficulty of breaking into this market.

Another key factor is inadequate infrastructure. Industry professionals believe the market has advanced too quickly, resulting in the overproduction of EVs without sufficient supporting infrastructure. Concerns about driving range and charging availability have grown among consumers, and the lack of specialist repair shops has resulted in high repair costs due to limited competition. Recently, Hertz sold 30,000 EVs from its rental fleet due to low rental demand and expensive repairs â€” a visible signal that consumer confidence has not fully caught up with the technology.

CONCLUSION

EVs will play a crucial role in moving towards a more sustainable future by lowering emissions and reducing reliance on fossil fuels. However, the recent slowdown in demand growth reveals real challenges the industry must confront. If governments and firms successfully address issues of price, infrastructure, and repairability, EVs have the potential to become the dominant mode of transportation globally.

HAVE A THINK

  • At what point does a government's role shift from encouraging EV adoption through subsidies to allowing the market to determine the pace of transition?

  • How does the high cost of EV batteries reflect the broader tension between technological progress and resource scarcity?

  • Could inadequate infrastructure become a permanent barrier to EV mass adoption, or is it simply a transitional problem that investment will solve?

title: China's Economic Woes
author: Chris John
excerpt: From Economic Powerhouse to Uncertain Future
body:
CHINA'S GOLDEN AGE

After the 2008 financial crisis, China maintained strong GDP growth, consistently achieving double-digit growth rates throughout much of the 2010s. While other major economies were slowing down, China appeared to be an unstoppable engine of global expansion. However, by 2022, the country's growth rate had declined sharply to just 3%. This significant drop raises serious concerns â€” and the question of whether this is a temporary setback or a sign of deeper structural problems for the world's second-largest economy.

THE START: SHADOW BANKING AND REAL ESTATE

Many experts point to 2016 as a turning point. It began when China introduced stricter regulations on its shadow banking sector â€” lending by non-traditional financial institutions. The government tightened oversight and reduced overall debt in the financial system. While these measures strengthened financial stability, they simultaneously constrained economic growth. According to the Reserve Bank of Australia, more than 60% of China's GDP in 2016 was linked to shadow financing.

The real estate sector was particularly dependent on this type of credit. As shadow financing became more restricted, cracks began to appear in a sector that had accounted for around 25% of China's GDP. The restriction of credit, combined with a collapse in post-COVID demand, led to widespread defaults among developers responsible for 40% of China's home sales. None larger than Evergrande, which by 2021 had accumulated total liabilities of $300 billion.

THE EVERGRANDE CRISIS

Once the most valuable real estate company in China, Evergrande defaulted on bond interest payments worth $82.5 million USD. The crisis reverberated through the broader housing market, with new housing starts falling by 57%. Growth slowed to 5.6% â€” the lowest in decades, excluding the pandemic years. The large debts owed to banks weakened confidence in China's financial sector, reducing both domestic consumer spending and the country's attractiveness to foreign investors.

THE CURRENT SITUATION

Unfortunately, no other sector has emerged to fill the gap left by the struggling housing market. In 2021, China introduced sweeping regulations targeting privately-owned companies, particularly in the technology and internet sector. This simultaneously expanded the role of state-owned enterprises, reducing business confidence as owners feared further regulation would erode revenues and profits â€” leading to a broader decline in private investment.

These factors combined to produce the largest price reduction in decades, with China's Consumer Price Index falling by 0.8% year-on-year in January â€” higher than the 0.5% predicted by Reuters. Prolonged deflation could further undermine confidence, creating a dangerous cycle of falling spending and declining economic activity.

There is, however, some cause for optimism. Analysts retain hope largely due to China's electric vehicle sector, with companies like BYD competing globally at comparatively low prices â€” BYD's cheapest offering starts at under $10,000, compared to Tesla's Model 3 at $32,000. However, recent tariffs introduced by Western countries risk slowing even this promising growth area.

CONCLUSION

Many factors have contributed to China's current economic difficulties: post-COVID demand weakness, the real estate collapse, and regulatory tightening that has weighed on private sector confidence. With China introducing its largest stimulus package since COVID-19, however, it would be premature to predict a prolonged economic downturn. Further data will be needed to understand whether this represents a temporary correction or a more fundamental shift in China's economic trajectory.

HAVE A THINK

  • To what extent did China's reliance on the real estate sector for growth make its current crisis inevitable?

  • How does the relationship between shadow banking and formal financial institutions illustrate the risks of regulatory arbitrage?

  • Can China's electric vehicle sector realistically replace real estate as the primary engine of domestic economic growth?

title: Economist of the Month: Milton Friedman
author: Christie Keeling
body:
WHO IS MILTON FRIEDMAN?

Milton Friedman (1912â€“2006) was an American economist and statistician who received the 1976 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his research on consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and the complexity of stabilisation policy. Born in Brooklyn, New York, to Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe, Friedman earned a scholarship to Rutgers University, where he studied mathematics and economics, before completing a master's degree at the University of Chicago in 1933 and a PhD from Columbia University in 1946.

Friedman became one of the most influential economists of the 20th century, reshaping global policy through his advocacy of free markets, monetary discipline, and limited government intervention.

FRIEDMAN'S THEORIES

During the 1960s, Friedman emerged as the main intellectual opponent of Keynesian government policies. He theorised that there existed a natural rate of unemployment, arguing that attempting to push unemployment below this rate would cause inflation to accelerate. He predicted what would come to be known as stagflation â€” the simultaneous occurrence of high inflation and high unemployment â€” well before the 1970s crisis made the term famous.

Friedman promoted monetarism: the view that a steady, small expansion of the money supply was the preferred policy framework, as opposed to the rapid and unpredictable changes associated with discretionary fiscal policy. His ideas on monetary policy, taxation, privatisation, and deregulation went on to influence government policy, particularly during the 1980s.

His most famous work, A Monetary History of the United States, 1867â€“1960, co-authored with Anna Schwartz, argued that poor monetary policy by the Federal Reserve was responsible for the severity of the Great Depression â€” overturning much of the previous consensus that had blamed inadequate fiscal responses or external shocks.

DID HIS THEORIES GAIN TRACTION?

Friedman's critique of Keynesian economics became highly influential during the 1970s, when rising inflation and economic stagnation began to expose the limitations of demand-management policies. As Keynesian models faltered, Friedman's monetarist approach gained traction across governments and central banks.

His ideas were instrumental in shaping the policies of Ronald Reagan in the United States and Margaret Thatcher in the United Kingdom, both of whom embraced free-market principles, deregulation, and a reduction in the size of government. His influence on central banking has also been lasting â€” his monetary theory shaped the Federal Reserve's response to the 2008 financial crisis.

OPPOSITIONS TO HIS THEORIES

Not all economists accepted Friedman's framework. Keynesians argued that monetary policy alone was insufficient during severe downturns â€” particularly in the presence of a liquidity trap â€” and that active fiscal policy remained essential. Post-Keynesian economists criticised what they saw as Friedman's oversimplification of complex financial dynamics, particularly his assumption that the velocity of money is stable. Others pointed out that the deregulatory policies inspired by his thinking contributed to the financial instability that culminated in the 2008 crisis.

HOW HIS WORK IS APPLIED TODAY

Friedman's legacy is visible across modern economic policy. Central banks around the world now operate with clear inflation targets â€” a direct reflection of his emphasis on monetary stability. His framework for understanding the Great Depression continues to inform how policymakers respond to financial crises, most visibly during the 2008 recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. His arguments for school choice, negative income tax, and free trade remain influential in contemporary policy debates, even where they remain contested.

HAVE A THINK

  • Was Friedman right that the Great Depression was primarily a monetary failure, or do fiscal and structural factors deserve more of the blame?

  • How far did the deregulatory policies inspired by Friedman's ideas contribute to the conditions that caused the 2008 financial crisis?

  • Is monetarism still a relevant framework for managing modern economies, or has the relationship between money supply and inflation become too unstable to rely on?

title: The Women Behind Our Economic History
author: Anna Vadasdi
body:
THE PERSISTENT MARGINALISATION OF WOMEN IN ECONOMICS

The marginalisation of women in financial and economic life has remained a troubling constant throughout modern history. Women's contributions to economic theory have consistently been overshadowed by their male counterparts â€” and it is precisely this pattern that makes acknowledgement so important.

ANNA SCHWARTZ AND THE CO-FOUNDING OF MONETARISM

We must begin with Anna Schwartz. She was the co-founder of monetarism â€” the framework of government control over the money supply that has become an essential tool for countries around the world to combat economic crises. A vivid example was seen during COVID-19, when central banks slashed interest rates to support economic activity and stabilise markets; the intellectual foundations for that response trace directly back to the work Schwartz helped build.

Yet in 1976, it was Milton Friedman who received the Nobel Prize for research on consumption analysis, monetary history, and the complexity of stabilisation policy â€” research built upon their joint work. Friedman himself acknowledged the imbalance, stating that "Anna did all the work, and I got all of the recognition." Despite this admission, Schwartz has never received the formal recognition her contributions warrant. Her story is a clear illustration of the persistent gender inequality that has long shaped this field.

MARY PALEY MARSHALL AND NEOCLASSICAL ECONOMICS

We should also discuss Mary Paley Marshall, whose husband Alfred Marshall is widely credited as the founder of neoclassical economics. Together, they co-authored The Economics of Industry â€” yet Alfred was awarded full credit for the work, propelling him to lasting greatness while Mary remained a modest and systematically suppressed voice in economic thought. The erasure of her contribution from mainstream history is a pattern repeated across the discipline: women's intellectual labour absorbed into the reputations of the men alongside whom they worked.

MOVING FORWARD

There has been a constant and well-documented battle for women in economics, rooted in the systematic non-recognition of their contributions to theory, research, and policy. Progress requires more than acknowledging individual cases â€” it demands a willingness to re-examine the historical record and ensure that the economists we celebrate reflect the full range of people who built this discipline.

HAVE A THINK

  • Why has the marginalisation of women in economics persisted even as women have gained greater access to higher education and professional life?

  • What does the story of Anna Schwartz and Milton Friedman reveal about how credit and recognition function within academic and intellectual institutions?

  • How might economic theory itself look different today if women like Mary Paley Marshall had received the same recognition as their male counterparts?
